transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-30
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Ethan Ramirez (Stellar AI CTO), Priya Singh (SRE), Liam O'Connor (ML Eng)

Summary:
- Deep dive on p95/p99 tail latency behavior for streaming vs non-streaming workloads
- Focus on KV cache hit patterns, batching, quantization impact, and network hops (VPC vs hosted)
- Action items: share benchmarks, run microbench on customer traces, schedule on-prem sizing

Topics covered:
- runtime hot paths and kernel selection
- continuous batching and per-request latency SLOs
- KV cache warmup and eviction patterns
- quantization tradeoffs (INT8/4bit) on p99
- network topology: VPC peering vs private deployment

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: okay hi everyone, thanks for taking the time, i'm Jordan from Redwood, i'm the AE on this account, with me is Maya our SE, she'll lead through the latency deep dive. could you quick intro?
[00:12] Ethan Ramirez: yeah hey all, ethan here, CTO at Stellar AI. we run real-time summarization and conversational agents, p50 is fine but p99 is killing us — users see spikes during heavy sessions.
[00:23] Priya Singh: priya here, SRE. our tail latency target is 350ms p99 for single-turn gen, and 150ms p95 for streaming token latency. right now we're seeing p99 spikes up to 1.2s.
[00:34] Maya Patel: thanks, that's helpful. quick note, i'll call out some shorthand — by streaming we mean token-by-token websocket / SSE streams, non-streaming is chunked response. does that map to what you have?
[00:43] Liam O'Connor: yep that's the setup. our infra: we front requests through our api gateway in GCP, then VPC peering to your hosted endpoints. some requests route to dedicated nodes in our test tenant.
[00:56] Jordan Lee: cool. maya, take it away on p99 drivers.
[01:00] Maya Patel: sure. high-level: p99 is often dominated by either queuing (batching delays) or long-tail compute on first-token generation when KV cache misses happen or quantized kernels hit worst-case paths. so we break it down into network, batching, kv, runtime kernels, and model size.
[01:18] Maya Patel: first network — your topology has an extra hop: your gateway -> GCP egress -> our hosted edge -> inference nodes. that adds variable ms. with VPC peering or private deployment you remove some of the variability.
[01:32] Priya Singh: right we were hoping VPC/private would help. what's typical delta?
[01:36] Maya Patel: median network delta maybe 10-40ms, but tail can be 100-200ms depending on cross-cloud egress and route flaps. we've seen p99 improve by ~80-150ms when customers move to VPC peering or private deployments — but compute side still matters.
[01:53] Ethan Ramirez: what about streaming vs non-streaming? streaming seems to have higher p95 because we flush small tokens quickly.
[01:59] Maya Patel: yes streaming exposes amortized overhead per-token — so the per-token overhead for network and syscall latency matters. for models with short tokens, p95 for streaming can be worse than non-streaming full-chunk return. however, non-streaming can hide variability by buffering but then first-byte latency (TTFB) suffers.
[02:16] Jordan Lee: quick interjection — our runtime supports continuous batching which tries to balance throughput vs latency; we can tune the batching window and max batch size per route.
[02:25] Maya Patel: exactly; if you set a high max batch and a small wait window you'll get queueing causing p99 spikes for small requests. we recommend per-route configs: low-latency routes use small batch windows (~2-5ms) and conservative batch caps.
[02:38] Liam O'Connor: in practice we've been using default batch settings, so maybe we're getting large variable queuing. is there a telemetry stream we can check?
[02:45] Maya Patel: yes we'll share the per-token latency traces and the batching histogram. Jordan will attach the benchmark spreadsheet.
[02:51] Priya Singh: moving to KV cache — our workload is multi-user with many distinct contexts, cache hit rate is low initially. how big an impact does a cold KV cache have on p99?
[03:02] Maya Patel: big. cold or churn-heavy KV caches cause the model to recompute key/value states for prefixes, so first-generation for a session can be 2-6x slower on p99. we measure warm hit improvement of 30-70% on tail depending on sequence lengths. eviction policy matters: LRU with session pinning helps for conversational workloads.
[03:21] Ethan Ramirez: session pinning meaning?
[03:23] Maya Patel: pinning keeps a user's KV entries on the same serving shard across requests to avoid repeated rebuilds. it can increase memory usage but reduces recompute and tail latency.
[03:29] Jordan Lee: also worth noting our runtime supports KV prefetching for likely next tokens when you can predict conversational flows, that can reduce cold-start p99.
[03:37] Priya Singh: okay how about quantization — we've been experimenting with 4-bit to save cost. any p99 tradeoffs?
[03:43] Maya Patel: quantization reduces compute latency on average but increases variance in some kernels, especially attention kernels with newer fused ops. in our benchmarks 4-bit can improve p50 by 20-40% but p99 sometimes regresses if kernels fall back to slower paths (dequant + higher-precision ops for stability). we recommend per-model profiling: if your prompt distribution includes long context and long sequences, p99 may suffer with aggressive quant. hybrid approach works: quantize for most traffic but route latency-sensitive routes to higher precision models.
[04:10] Liam O'Connor: does Redwood's routing support that per route? like route by SLO?
[04:13] Maya Patel: yes, smart routing can route by policy — you can set a latency SLO and route to dedicated higher-precision pools when exceeding budget, or fallback to compact models for cost windows.
[04:22] Ethan Ramirez: can you show any real numbers from similar customers?
[04:25] Maya Patel: sure — we have a small graph in the sheet, but high level: Customer A (realtime chat) moved to VPC peering + session pinning + tuned batching and saw p99 drop from 1.0s to 420ms; p95 went from 220ms to 140ms. Customer B (long docs) used hybrid quant routing and saw p50 improve 35% while p99 stayed within 10% after kernel tuning. I'll attach the detailed traces.
[04:50] Priya Singh: okay network-wise, we cannot fully move to private on day one — we need to validate via VPC peering. does Redwood provide any tooling to run microbench from our VPC into your endpoints?
[04:59] Maya Patel: yes, we provide a microbench container you can run that replays traces and captures per-hop latency. we'll give you an image and a sample config.
[05:07] Jordan Lee: we'll also share a minimal k6/load runner script and the p95/p99 spreadsheet.
[05:12] Ethan Ramirez: good. a couple more things — how do you instrument streaming token latency? we need token-level traces, not only request-level.
[05:19] Maya Patel: runtime emits token-level spans in the trace logs, we can export those to your tracing (OTel) or share raw logs. streaming per-token overhead includes network + serialization + runtime token dispatch. typical per-token overhead we see is 5-20ms extra compared to bulk non-streaming, depends on payload size and network RTT.
[05:38] Priya Singh: and on our side, we use private peering but still go via an internal API gateway which sometimes introduces head-of-line blocking. any suggestions?
[05:46] Maya Patel: isolate the inference path from heavy proxies, use straight TCP flow with keep-alives, and prefer HTTP/2 or websocket streaming to reduce handshake overhead. also ensure your gateway isn't applying global rate-limiting that batches bursts.
[05:58] Liam O'Connor: question about sequence length and kernel selection — we see p99 tail when users paste long docs. does Redwood recompile kernels on the fly?
[06:05] Maya Patel: our runtime chooses kernels based on observed seq-length distributions and will pick slower but memory-friendly kernels for very long sequences. long-tail sequences can cause memory pressure and GPU spill to CPU, which is a big p99 offender. we recommend capping max length server-side or routing long-seq requests to dedicated large-memory nodes.
[06:22] Ethan Ramirez: how do we handle bursty diurnal traffic and autoscale without hurting p99?
[06:27] Jordan Lee: dedicated pools with warm standby and predictive autoscale helps; you can configure burst capacity and pre-warm policies. completely cold spin-up will always be a p99 hit.
[06:36] Priya Singh: any best practices for KV size & eviction to minimize p99?
[06:40] Maya Patel: tune per-shard KV size to match active session footprint, pin high-value sessions, use LRU with TTL, and monitor eviction rates. if eviction rate crosses a threshold (e.g., >10% per minute) you'll see p99 increases.
[06:52] Ethan Ramirez: curious about TTFB vs last-token latency tradeoffs — our product is OK with slower final tokens but users complain about first-token delays.
[07:00] Maya Patel: then prioritize first-token latency: use smaller batching windows, keep a pool of warmed KV contexts for likely prompts, and use fast-path kernels for first-token. you can stream pre-emptive tokens if appropriate.
[07:11] Jordan Lee: quick clarification on metrics: we recommend tracking client-observed p99, server processing p99, and network delta separately. that helps isolate root cause.
[07:20] Priya Singh: agreed. can you walk through an example failure mode — e.g., what happens if KV misses and we also hit a slow network spike?
[07:28] Maya Patel: chain of events: network spike adds 120ms; KV miss causes additional 200-400ms for recompute; if batching window is high you might add 50-200ms queue. combined you can exceed 1s at p99. mitigation: reduce batching for critical routes, pin sessions, prefetch, and move to VPC to remove network variability.
[07:48] Ethan Ramirez: do you have an example config we'd copy?
[07:51] Maya Patel: yes, we'll attach recommended per-route config: low-latency route: batch_window_ms=3, max_batch=8, enable_session_pinning=true; high-throughput route: batch_window_ms=12, max_batch=64.
[08:03] Liam O'Connor: about quantization again — you mentioned kernel fallbacks causing regression. is there a way to detect fallback occurrences in logs?
[08:11] Maya Patel: yes logs include kernel variant tags and a "fallback_count" metric per request. we'll add that column to the benchmark sheet.
[08:18] Priya Singh: what's the overhead for tracing token-level spans?
[08:22] Maya Patel: minimal, around 1-2% overhead if you sample correctly. full trace export at 100% can add overhead, so we recommend sampling and short retention for production traces.
[08:33] Jordan Lee: i want to call out pricing tradeoffs — if you move critical routes to dedicated higher-precision nodes p99 improves but cost increases. we can model the trade in the spreadsheet.
[08:43] Ethan Ramirez: fair. can you run a microbench on our sample traces and share the p95/p99 delta for streaming vs non-streaming?
[08:50] Maya Patel: yes, please send the traces — preferably anonymized — and we'll run the kv microbench with and without session pinning and with 4-bit vs 8-bit quant to show p95/p99.
[08:59] Priya Singh: we'll need security docs for VPC peering — SOC2, PCI not relevant but ISO, audit logs, SSO.
[09:06] Jordan Lee: we'll send the security datasheet and SAML/KMS integrations.
[09:10] Ethan Ramirez: ok final wrap, can we summarize next steps?
[09:13] Jordan Lee: sure. recap: 1) Jordan sends benchmark spreadsheet, per-route config templates, security datasheet (due 12/3). 2) Priya sends sample prompt set and traces (due 12/2). 3) Maya runs KV microbench and shares logs (due 12/6). 4) schedule on-prem sizing / peering follow-up for week of 12/7.
[09:33] Priya Singh: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[09:36] Ethan Ramirez: thanks, really helpful.
[09:38] Jordan Lee: thanks all, we'll follow up with the artifacts.
